1.note: Isaiah is using the possessive form **my God** to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are God to me]

Here, **your name** represents “who Yahweh is and his reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you and your reputation]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [making plans long ago, and carrying them out with faithfulness and trustworthiness]

The terms **faithfulness** and **trustworthiness** mean similar things. Isaiah is using masculine and feminine forms of the same word for emphasis. If your language has masculine and feminine forms of a word with this same meaning, it would be appropriate to use them here in your translation. If not, you could express the emphasis in another way, for example, by using a single phrase. Alternate translation: [total faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trustworthiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [trustworthy deeds]

3.note: Here **city** and **nations** represent the people who live there. See the UST.

It might seem that the expression **to him** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [a fortress for the needy in distress]

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh were **a shelter from the storm, a shade from the heat**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a place that protects them from storms and heat] or [a source of protection from storms and heat]

Isaiah is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [terrifying people]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a storm against a wall** is powerful and destructive, so is **the breath of the terrible**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the force of the violent is as powerful and destructive as a storm against a wall]

5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **heat in a dry place** is overwhelming and inescapable, so is the oppression of ruthless people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like the inescapable heat of a desert]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uproar**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the disturbing noise that foreigners cause]

Even though Isaiah is addressing Yahweh directly, Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh in the third person as **He** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [Yahweh silences]

Isaiah is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. See how you translated the similar expression in 25:4. Alternate translation: [terrible people]

6.note: Here, **lees** represents “wine on the lees,” implying the most flavorful wine. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a feast of aged wine]

7.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the **face of the covering** were something that Yahweh could **swallow up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. 7.q: הַ⁠לּ֥וֹט הַ⁠לּ֖וֹט עַל כָּל הָֽ⁠עַמִּ֑ים וְ⁠הַ⁠מַּסֵּכָ֥ה הַ⁠נְּסוּכָ֖ה עַל כָּל הַ⁠גּוֹיִֽם

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

9.note: The pronoun **one** refers to people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And people will say]

Alternate translation: [when that happens]
Isaiah is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See the UST.

The speakers are using the term **Behold** to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look] or [Listen]

The speakers are using the possessive form **our God** to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom they worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is God to us]

9.q: אֱלֹהֵ֥י⁠נוּ זֶ֛ה קִוִּ֥ינוּ ל֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠יֽוֹשִׁיעֵ֑⁠נוּ זֶ֤ה יְהוָה֙ קִוִּ֣ינוּ ל֔⁠וֹ נָגִ֥ילָה וְ⁠נִשְׂמְחָ֖ה בִּ⁠ישׁוּעָתֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [this is our God; we waited for him, and he saved us. Indeed, this is Yahweh; we waited for him, let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation]

The terms **be glad** and **rejoice** mean similar things. The speakers are using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [let us rejoice joyfully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because he has saved us]

10.note: Here, **the hand of Yahweh** represents “Yahweh’s power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s power]

10.q: וְ⁠נָ֤דוֹשׁ מוֹאָב֙ תַּחְתָּ֔י⁠ו כְּ⁠הִדּ֥וּשׁ מַתְבֵּ֖ן ב⁠מי מַדְמֵנָֽה
10.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **straw** is completely destroyed when **trampled in a dunghill**, so Moab will be completely defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and Moab will be completely destroyed in its place, just as straw is completely destroyed when it is trampled in a dunghill]

The expression **Moab will be trampled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will trample Moab in its place]

The expression **straw is trampled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as someone tramples straw in a dunghill]

11.q: וּ⁠פֵרַ֤שׂ יָדָי⁠ו֙ בְּ⁠קִרְבּ֔⁠וֹ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֛ר יְפָרֵ֥שׂ הַ⁠שֹּׂחֶ֖ה לִ⁠שְׂח֑וֹת

If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it, just as a swimmer spreads his hands in order to swim]
The pronoun **he** refers to Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Moab will spread out his hands]
The pronoun **he** in this clause refers to Yahweh, and **his** refers to Moab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will bring low Moab’s pride]

Isaiah has been referring to Moab in the third person, but now he addresses Moab directly with **your walls**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the third person consistently. Alternate translation: [their walls]
